ta-l1d2q1-d1e97.summary: A divisio textus framing the whole Sentences and then Distinction 2. Since sacred doctrine concerns divine things, and things are divine as related to God as principle or end ('I am the alpha and the omega'), the work treats things as they go forth from God (Books I–II) and as they return to him as end (Books III–IV). Alternatively, following Lombard's own plan, it treats things (enjoyable, usable, and what orders the usable to the enjoyable) and then signs. Book I treats the procession of persons in unity of essence, which is the cause of the procession of creatures in diversity of essence. It considers first the Trinity and then the attributes of knowledge, power, and will that complete divine causality (Dist. 35 onward). Thomas maps Distinction 2 as Lombard's account of the right way to investigate the Trinity: the investigators' purity, reverence, and mutual charity, the Catholic doctors' intention, and the order of proceeding from authorities. Lombard then demonstrates the Trinity in unity from Old and New Testament authorities. Thomas announces five articles: on the unity of the divine essence; on attributes in that unity; on whether the conceptual distinctions of attributes are in God or only in the mind; on whether that unity allows a plurality of persons; and on whether that plurality is real.
claims: Theology treats things as they go forth from God as principle and return to him as end.
The procession of the persons in unity of essence is the cause of the procession of creatures in diversity of essence.
Book I treats the Trinity first and then the attributes (knowledge, power, will) that complete divine causality toward creatures.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e170.summary: First objection against positing one God. According to the Philosopher, only one thing proceeds from what is one, first, and simple. But many distinct perfections (wisdom, goodness, peace) are participated in creatures, so they seem to come from many first principles. This was the error of the pagans, who had one god of wisdom, another goddess of peace, and so on (Dionysius).
claims: From one simple first principle only one thing proceeds.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e179.summary: Second objection. A thing is perfect when it can produce something like itself in nature (Metaphysics 5). The divine essence is most perfect, so it seems able to produce another essence like itself, and there would be several divine essences.
claims: A thing is perfect when it can produce its like in nature.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e188.summary: Third objection. Prime matter, pure potency, is one, and forms are fewer the closer they are to matter (four elemental forms, then the many forms of mixed bodies). Plurality thus increases with distance from matter. Since God is most removed from matter, the divine nature should be most multiplied.
claims: Plurality of forms increases with remoteness from matter.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e192.summary: Sed contra. Every nature found in many things according to prior and posterior must derive from one first in which it is perfectly found, as all heat derives from fire, the hottest. Being is found in things according to prior and posterior, so there must be one first and most perfect being from which all beings have their being, namely God.
claims: A nature found by degrees in many derives from one first in which it is perfectly realized.
There is one first and most perfect being from which all beings have being.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e195.summary: Second sed contra. If there were several gods distinct in essence, their essences would differ by an essential difference, as in genus or species. That difference either pertains to goodness or it does not. If not, the god possessing it would not be pure goodness. If so, the god lacking it would not be perfect in goodness. God must be the highest good, both pure and perfect, so there cannot be several gods.
claims: God as highest good must be both pure and perfect in goodness, which excludes a plurality of gods distinguished by a difference.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e198.summary: Anticipates a reply: perhaps the difference is the same in species but different in number. But what is of one species is divided in number only through matter or some potentiality, so God would contain potentiality and be a diminished and dependent being, which contradicts the notion of a first being.
claims: Numerical multiplication within a species requires matter or potentiality.
A first being cannot contain potentiality.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e201.summary: Third sed contra. If a thing's being and quiddity do not differ, its essence cannot be participated unless its being is participated too. But when an essence is divided by participation, it is shared in concept, not in the same being. So the essence of that in which essence and being are identical cannot be divided or multiplied, and God is such, since otherwise his being would be acquired from another. The divinity cannot be multiplied.
claims: Where essence and esse are identical, the essence cannot be multiplied by participation.
In God essence and esse are identical; otherwise his being would be acquired from another.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e204.summary: Thomas's determination. Since every multitude proceeds from some unity (Dionysius), the multitude of the universe must be traced back to one first principle of beings, God. Faith presupposes this and reason demonstrates it.
claims: The multitude of the universe must be reduced to one first principle, God.
The unicity of God is both presupposed by faith and demonstrated by reason.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e210.summary: Reply to the first objection. The goodnesses participated in creatures differ conceptually but are ordered to one another, one including and being founded on another (understanding includes living, living includes being), so they reduce to one principle. Even if they were unordered, the unity of the first principle would stand, since what is united in the cause is multiplied in the effects. The first principle, one and simple in reality, contains many conceptually distinct perfections (wisdom, life) according to which really different perfections are caused in creatures.
claims: Participated perfections are ordered and reduce to one principle.
What is united in the cause is multiplied in the effects.
The first principle, though really simple, contains many conceptual perfections.
concepts: unity of cause and multiplicity of effects

ta-l1d2q1-d1e214.summary: Reply to the second objection. It belongs to the perfection of the divine essence that no essence can be like and equal to it. Any essence produced by it would depend on it for its being and so contain potentiality, which would distinguish it from God, who is pure act. Not everything that belongs to a creature's nobility belongs to the Creator's, which exceeds it beyond proportion. Being fierce ennobles a dog but would debase a human (Dionysius).
claims: No essence can be equal to the divine essence, since a produced essence would have dependent, potential being.
The perfections of creatures are not simply transferable to God.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e220.summary: Reply to the third objection. A simple principle has the character of unity. Prime matter is numerically one through the removal of all distinguishing forms, not through a form of its own. By the same reasoning pure and first act is one, and it cannot be multiplied as matter is by the coming of forms; it is wholly incapable of diversity.
claims: Pure act, like prime matter, is one by its simplicity but, unlike matter, cannot be multiplied.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e232.summary: First objection against a plurality of attributes. What is most one is most removed from plurality, as the whitest is what is least mixed with black. The divine essence is supremely one, the principle of all unity, so it admits no plurality of attributes.
claims: What is supremely one excludes all plurality.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e238.summary: Second objection. What is one and simple has one operation, but different attributes have different operations (knowing, willing). So God has no diversity of attributes.
claims: One simple essence has one operation.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e241.summary: Sed contra from Augustine. Whatever it is simply better to be than not to be must be attributed to God, and wisdom, goodness, and the like are such.
claims: Whatever it is simply better to have than not must be attributed to God.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e248.summary: Second sed contra. Whatever is so in a qualified sense originates from what is so absolutely. Things are found perfect in their kind to greater or lesser degrees, so there must be something perfect absolutely. That is God, in whom are found all the nobilities of all genera (the Philosopher and the Commentator).
claims: What is perfect in a qualified sense presupposes something perfect absolutely.
God is perfect simply, containing the nobilities of all genera.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e257.summary: Thomas's determination. All the being and goodness of creatures comes from the Creator, while their imperfection comes from their being from nothing. A cause has what it causes in a more excellent way. So all creaturely nobilities exist in God in the noblest way, without imperfection, and what is diverse in creatures is one in him. Wisdom, goodness, and the like are each the divine essence and are one in reality. But each is in God according to its truest concept, and the concept of wisdom is not that of goodness, so they differ in concept, not merely on the side of the reasoner but from the property of the thing itself. God is therefore not a wholly equivocal cause: he produces effects like his form analogically, not univocally, and he is the exemplar of things through his attributes as well as through his ideas. Thomas rejects the view that the attributes differ only by what they connote in creatures. The cause does not receive from the effect; God was truly wise from eternity even without creatures; and the attribute names are not synonyms.
claims: All creaturely perfections pre-exist in God in a more eminent way, without imperfection, and are one in reality.
The divine attributes differ conceptually because of the reality itself, not merely through the reasoner.
God is an analogical, not equivocal, cause and is exemplar through his attributes as well as his ideas.
Attributes do not differ merely by connoting different creaturely effects.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e263.summary: Reply to the first objection. The plurality of attributes in no way prejudices God's supreme unity, since what is many in others is one in him. Only a conceptual plurality remains, which does not oppose real unity but necessarily follows from it when perfection is also present.
claims: The conceptual plurality of attributes follows necessarily from real unity combined with perfection.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e266.summary: Reply to the second objection. God's operation is his essence, so it is one in reality but multiplied by diverse concepts, just as the one essence is considered under many conceptual attributes.
claims: God's operation is identical with his essence and is one in reality, though conceptually many.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e278.summary: First objection that the conceptual plurality of attributes is only in the reasoning intellect. Dionysius says the theologians' hymns divide the divine names according to the good processions of the Thearchy. So the plurality comes from the diversity of effects by which our intellect knows and names God, not from God.
claims: The divine names are divided according to God's diverse processions into creatures.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e287.summary: Second objection. Dionysius says that if someone seeing God understood what they saw, they did not see God himself but something of his. So the concepts by which the divine names differ correspond to nothing in God, only to his creatures.
claims: What we understand of God is not God himself but something of his.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e296.summary: Third objection. The Commentator (Averroes) says the multiplicity these names express is in God according to the intellect and in no way according to reality.
claims: The multiplicity of divine names is only in the intellect.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e303.summary: Fourth objection. Whatever is in God is God. If the distinguishing concepts are in God they are God, and God is one and simple, so as in God they are not many.
claims: Whatever is in God is God.
concepts: quidquid est in Deo est Deus

ta-l1d2q1-d1e306.summary: Fifth objection. What is one in every way cannot be the root of any multitude within it. The divine essence is one in every way, so the plurality of concepts is rooted only in the intellect.
claims: What is one in every way cannot be the root of a multitude existing in it.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e309.summary: Sixth objection from John Damascene: in God all things are one except ingenerateness, generation, and procession. So the attributes, as they are in God, have no plurality.
claims: In God everything is one except the personal properties.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e312.summary: Sed contra. Dionysius, the Philosopher, and the Commentator call God perfect as comprehending all things and all perfections of every genus in himself. This perfection belongs to God in reality and not only in the intellect, so the attributes expressing it are in reality.
claims: God's perfection, comprehending all perfections, is real and not merely conceptual.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e324.summary: Second sed contra. According to Dionysius, creatures are like God insofar as they imitate him, though imperfectly, and this imitation is by participation in the attributes. That would be impossible unless wisdom and goodness were in God according to their proper concepts.
claims: Creaturely likeness to God through participated attributes requires that the attributes be in God according to their proper concepts.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e330.summary: Third sed contra. Wisdom is not said equivocally of God and creatures, otherwise created wisdom would not lead to knowledge of uncreated wisdom. So the concept of wisdom said of both is somehow one, by analogy and not univocity. Since the concepts of wisdom, goodness, and power differ in creatures, they also differ as said of God.
claims: Perfection terms are said of God and creatures analogically, not equivocally.
The diversity of attribute concepts in creatures carries over analogically to God.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e334.summary: Fourth sed contra, from the personal relations. God is truly Father as he is truly wise. The concept of paternity, which is really in God, is not the concept of divinity, yet this plurality of concepts does not destroy simplicity, since essence and paternity are really the same. So positing the concepts of wisdom and goodness in God, distinct in concept but one in reality, does not destroy simplicity either.
claims: Paternity is really in God and conceptually distinct from the essence without compromising simplicity.
By parity, attributes can be really one and conceptually distinct in God.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e337.summary: Rebuts a disanalogy. One might say relations differ from the essence because they belong to another category, whereas absolute attributes belong to substance. But a divine relation can be compared both to its correlative, which makes it 'toward another', and to the essence, with which it is really identical. Its belonging to another category concerns only its relation to the correlative, so wisdom and paternity stand in the same relation to the essence.
claims: A divine relation has a twofold comparison: to its correlative and to the essence.
As compared to the essence, relation and absolute attributes stand alike.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e340.summary: Thomas's extended determination, which he says the understanding of all of Book I depends on. The attributes are one in reality and differ in concept, and this conceptual difference is grounded in the thing as well as the reasoner. He examines four points. (1) What a ratio is: what the intellect grasps of a name's signification, i.e. the definition where there is one. 'Ratio' itself is a second-intention name. (2) How a ratio is said to be in a thing: not as the concept itself, which is in the mind, but because something in the thing corresponds to it as signified to sign. Concepts relate to things in three ways. Some are likenesses of things and have an immediate foundation in them (man). Some follow on our mode of understanding and have a remote foundation (genus, mathematical abstractions). Some have no foundation at all (chimera). (3) Whether the rationes of the attributes are in God. Avicenna and Maimonides hold that God is esse without essence and that attribute names are verified only by negation or causality; it follows that they are equivocal and the rationes are only in the intellect. Dionysius and Anselm hold that every creaturely perfection exists eminently in God, with universality, fullness, and unity, so our concepts are true though deficient likenesses of God with a proximate foundation in him. Thomas reconciles the two views. The first considers the creaturely things on which the names are imposed (qualities, non-subsistents), which are far from God; the second considers the modes of perfection signified, which God has supremely. So the rationes are truly in God. (4) Whether the plurality of rationes is only from our intellect. It arises because God exceeds our intellect, which cannot grasp his perfection in one concept, both because it learns from creatures and because what is one in God is multiplied in any created reception. In heaven God might be given one name ('his name shall be one', Zech. 14:9), but even the blessed would form many concepts, since no created concept represents God fully; only the uncreated Word does. So the plurality comes partly from our intellect and partly from God, whose full perfection, not any real plurality, corresponds to all these concepts and makes each name truly and properly said of him, even had he created nothing.
claims: A ratio is what the intellect conceives as a name's signification, and is 'in the thing' when something in the thing corresponds to it.
Concepts are founded in things immediately, remotely (via our mode of understanding), or not at all.
The views of Avicenna/Maimonides and of Dionysius/Anselm on divine attributes are reconcilable when the bases of their claims are considered.
The rationes of the attributes are truly in God, with a proximate foundation in his full perfection.
The plurality of rationes arises because God's perfection exceeds every created concept; only the uncreated Word represents him perfectly.
God would be truly wise and good even if he had never created anything.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e364.summary: Reply to the first objection. Dionysius means that God is named, manifested, and praised according to the goodnesses he pours into creatures. He does not mean that those rationes are verified of God because he pours them out. The reverse is true: although the condition of a cause is known from its effects, it is not verified because of them.
claims: The condition of a cause is known from its effects but is not true of the cause because of the effects.
concepts: order of knowing vs. order of being

ta-l1d2q1-d1e370.summary: Reply to the second objection. Our intellect does not refer what it conceives of goodness or wisdom to God as if it were in him in the way it is conceived, which would be to comprehend his wisdom. It understands divine goodness, to which its concept is somewhat similar, as lying beyond the concept. Through such concepts God is not seen as he is in himself but is understood to be above the intellect. This is Dionysius's meaning.
claims: Our concepts of God are similar to him yet he is understood to exceed them.
Through such concepts God is understood as above the intellect, not seen as he is.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e376.summary: Reply to the third objection. The multiplicity of attributes is in no way placed in God as a real multiplicity. But by his simple perfection he corresponds to the multitude of attributes, so that they are truly said of him; this is the Commentator's intent.
claims: God's simple perfection corresponds to the many attributes without any real multiplicity in him.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e383.summary: Reply to the fourth objection. The ratio of 'man' is not in a man as some thing in him. It is in the intellect as in a subject and in the man as what supports its truth. Likewise the ratio of divine goodness is in the intellect as subject and in God as what corresponds by likeness and makes it true. The objection misunderstands the claim.
claims: A ratio exists in the intellect as its subject and in the thing as the foundation of its truth.
concepts: subject vs. foundation of a concept

ta-l1d2q1-d1e386.summary: Reply to the fifth objection. To be 'rooted' in something means metaphorically to have firmness from it. Understood rationes have two firmnesses: of their being, which they have from the intellect as subject, and of their truth, which they have from the thing they conform to. So the rationes of the attributes are rooted in the intellect as to their being and in the divine essence as to their truth, which does not conflict with divine simplicity.
claims: Concepts have firmness of being from the intellect and firmness of truth from the thing.
The attribute rationes are rooted in the divine essence as to their truth.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e389.summary: Reply to the sixth objection. In God everything is one in reality except ingenerateness, generation, and procession, which constitute really distinct persons. It does not follow that everything else is one in concept, and Boethius's dictum that only relation multiplies the Trinity concerns real plurality. Something is one in reality and many in concept when one thing corresponds to diverse true concepts. A point, for example, is truly conceived in itself, as a centre, or as the beginning of lines. The concepts are in the intellect as subject and in the point as the foundation of their truth, though, like every example in divine matters, this one is imperfect.
claims: Only the personal properties introduce real plurality in God; the attributes are conceptually many.
A thing is one in reality and many in concept when one reality grounds diverse true concepts.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e405.summary: First objection against a plurality of persons in the one essence. In all creatures, multiplying supposits multiplies the essence numerically (humanity differs in Socrates and Plato). Creatures are modeled on God, and the divine essence cannot be multiplied (art. 1), so there cannot be several supposits or persons in God.
claims: In creatures the multiplication of supposits entails numerical multiplication of the essence.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e408.summary: Second objection. When two things are identical, if one is multiplied or communicated so is the other. In God that by which he is and that which he is, essence and supposit, are identical. So if the essence is not multiplied, neither are the supposits.
claims: In God essence and supposit are identical.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e411.summary: Third objection. A specific nature is multiplied in many individuals because it cannot have its whole perfection in one corruptible individual; incorruptibles, like the sun, have one individual per species. The divine nature has all perfection in one supposit, so a plurality of supposits would be pointless and cannot exist in God.
claims: Specific natures are multiplied in individuals only to preserve the species against corruption.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e415.summary: Sed contra arguments from perfection. Good is self-diffusive (Dionysius), and God is supremely good, so he communicates himself supremely. He does not do so in creatures, which do not receive his whole goodness, so there must be a perfect communication of his whole goodness, which can only be within the unity of essence. The same follows from the perfection of divine beatitude, since the highest joy requires companionship, and from the perfection of divine charity, a gratuitous love tending toward another. Supreme love requires a supremely lovable beloved, which a creature is not.
claims: The good is self-diffusive, so supreme goodness requires a perfect self-communication within the divine essence.
Perfect beatitude and perfect charity seem to require a distinct, supremely lovable beloved within God.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e421.summary: Thomas's determination. A plurality of supposits or persons in the unity of essence must be granted without any hesitation, not because of the arguments given, which do not conclude necessarily, but because of the truth of faith.
claims: The plurality of persons in the unity of essence is to be held on faith.
Rational arguments for the Trinity are not necessarily demonstrative.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e424.summary: Reply to the first objection. In a creature, essence and being differ, and the essence has being only in relation to the one who has it. When a created essence is communicated, it is communicated only in its concept and not in its being. The divine essence is its being, so when it is communicated its being is communicated too. It is one not only in concept but in being, and so it can be numerically one in several supposits. Creatures, though modeled on God, fall short of representing him.
claims: A created essence is communicated only in concept, since its being belongs to one possessor.
Because the divine essence is its esse, it can be numerically one in several supposits.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e427.summary: Reply to the second objection. Essence and supposit in God are really the same but differ in concept, as the attributes do; the Commentator notes that 'life' and 'living' are not synonyms in God. Being communicated is contrary to the concept of a supposit but not to the concept of an essence, so one essence is communicated to several supposits.
claims: Essence and supposit in God are really identical but conceptually distinct.
Communicability belongs to the concept of essence, incommunicability to that of supposit.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e433.summary: Reply to the third objection. The necessity of the end is conditional, by supposition, and is not sought in what is absolutely necessary, still less in what is necessary of itself. The plurality of supposits in God is not for an end but necessarily exists for its own sake, God being the end of all things. It cannot be called vain, since the vain is what is ordered to an end it does not attain.
claims: The plurality of divine persons is necessary of itself and not for the sake of an end.
Only what fails to attain its end is vain.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e445.summary: First objection that the plurality of persons is only conceptual. Damascene says the three persons are the same in reality and distinguished in concept and cognition.
claims: Damascene says the persons are one in reality and distinct in concept.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e454.summary: Second objection. Augustine says the persons are distinguished in nothing absolute, only in what is relative. A 'thing' (res) is absolute, not relative, so the persons are not three things and their distinction is not real.
claims: The persons are distinguished only by what is relative, and 'thing' denotes something absolute.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e460.summary: Third objection. The persons are distinguished by properties, which add nothing to the essence in reality, only in concept. So the distinction they make is only conceptual.
claims: Personal properties add to the essence only conceptually.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e464.summary: Fourth objection. Paternity and essence differ in concept just as wisdom and essence do. If that were enough for a real distinction of supposits, the attributes would also distinguish supposits, and there would be as many persons as attributes, which is absurd.
claims: If conceptual difference from the essence sufficed for real distinction, attributes would multiply persons.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e467.summary: Sed contra from Augustine. The things to be enjoyed are the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, so the three persons are several things, and their plurality is real.
claims: The three persons are several things (res).

ta-l1d2q1-d1e476.summary: Second sed contra. A conceptual distinction is not enough to distinguish supposits, since one human being can have many concepts, and 'supposit' signifies something real. If there were only a conceptual distinction in God, there would be no true plurality of persons, which is heretical.
claims: A distinction of reason does not suffice for a distinction of supposits.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e479.summary: Thomas's determination. Saying that the persons are distinguished only in concept sounds like Sabellian heresy, so the plurality of persons must simply be called real. The personal property, the distinguishing relation, is really the same as the divine essence and differs in concept, as the attributes do. But the concept of relation is to be referred to another. A divine relation can therefore be considered in two ways: as compared to the essence, where the difference is only conceptual; or as compared to its correlative, where by the proper concept of relation it is really distinct from it. The persons are distinguished by the relation's comparison to its opposite correlative, not to the essence, so the plurality of persons is real.
claims: The plurality of divine persons is real, not merely conceptual.
A divine relation is conceptually distinct from the essence but really distinct from its opposed correlative.
The persons are distinguished through the opposition of relations.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e482.summary: Reply to the first objection. Damascene's 'ratione' means 'by relation', and relation is called a ratio in its comparison to the essence.
claims: Damascene's 'in concept' should be read as 'by relation'.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e491.summary: Reply to the second objection. 'Thing' (res) is a transcendental and so applies to both absolutes and relatives. There is an essential res, in which the persons do not differ, and a relative or personal res, by which they are distinguished.
claims: 'Res' is transcendental, applying to both absolute and relative.
The persons are distinguished as relative things.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e495.summary: Reply to the third objection. Although relation compared to the essence is only conceptually distinct, compared to its correlative it is a thing and really distinguishes itself from it.
claims: Relation compared to its correlative is a res really distinct from it.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e498.summary: Reply to the fourth objection. Wisdom differs in concept from the other attributes but is not opposed to any of them, since it is compatible with goodness and the rest in the same subject. So it cannot distinguish supposits as opposed relations can. As divine wisdom really produces effects of wisdom because its concept is true, relation makes a true distinction because its concept is truly preserved.
claims: Only opposed relations distinguish supposits; non-opposed attributes cannot.
The true concept of relation, preserved in God, grounds a true distinction.

ta-l1d2q1-d1e511.summary: An expositio textus of Distinction 2 glossing a series of Lombard's phrases. 'Substance or essence' is noted as improper (cf. Dist. 8). 'Believed and understood' traces the genesis of faith: preaching, assent, and then understanding ('unless you believe, you will not understand'). The 'purification of minds' takes three forms: from sense images for natural knowledge, from errors for faith, and from all guilt and misery for vision through essence. The excellence of the divine light is likened to the owl's eye before the sun. The 'justice of faith' means general justice, with faith as the first movement of justification. Augustine's retractations are explained, including why 'is' must be predicated plurally of the three persons, since it signifies substance by way of act and acts are numbered by supposits. The remarks that no error is more dangerous and nothing more fruitful are glossed: the Trinity is the foundation and the fruit of faith. Ambrose's dictum that 'God' names the nature and 'Lord' names the power is defended against Damascene's etymologies of Theos, by distinguishing what a name is imposed from and what it is imposed to signify; lordship is a relation founded on power. Augustine's and Hilary's readings of 'Let us make man in our image and likeness' are compared: Augustine finds plurality in 'us' and unity in 'image', while Hilary finds both in each word, taking likeness and image as relations between persons. Hilary's terms (diversity, singularity, solitude; likeness, plurality, distinction) are explained, and the Proverbs 8 wisdom passage is glossed of the Son, with possession, conception, birth, delight, and play read as features of divine wisdom. The two living creatures of Habakkuk and the tongs of Isaiah 6 signify the two testaments.
claims: Faith proceeds from hearing to assent to understanding.
Different kinds of knowledge of God require different purifications of the mind.
'Is' is predicated plurally of the three persons because it signifies substance by way of act, and acts are numbered by supposits.
'God' signifies the divine nature, though imposed from an operation; 'Lord' is a relation founded on power.
Hilary and Augustine read Genesis 1:26 differently as evidence for unity of essence and plurality of persons.
concepts: appropriation of wisdom to the Son

ta-l1d2q1-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 2 sets the whole Sentences within an exitus–reditus scheme (things going forth from God as principle, returning to him as end) and situates Book I as the treatment of the procession of persons in unity of essence, cause of the procession of creatures. It maps Lombard's account of how to investigate the Trinity and his scriptural proofs, and announces five articles on divine unity, attributes, their conceptual distinction, the plurality of persons, and the reality of that plurality.
claims: Theology treats things as they proceed from God and return to him.
The procession of persons is the cause of the procession of creatures.

ta-l1d2q1-Dd1e162.summary: Article 1 asks whether there is one God. Objections argue from the many participated perfections in creatures, from perfection as self-production, and from the increase of plurality with distance from matter. The sed contra arguments prove God's unicity from the degrees of being, from God as pure and perfect good, from the need for potentiality in any numerical multiplication, and from the identity of essence and esse. Thomas determines that every multitude reduces to one first principle, which faith presupposes and reason demonstrates. The replies show that participated perfections are ordered and are united in their cause. No essence can be equal to the divine essence, since anything produced would be dependent and potential, and pure act, unlike prime matter, cannot be multiplied.
claims: God is one, as faith holds and reason demonstrates.
Where essence and esse are identical, the essence cannot be multiplied.
Many perfections in creatures are united in their simple cause.

ta-l1d2q1-Dd1e224.summary: Article 2 asks whether there is a plurality of attributes in the one divine essence. Against the objections from supreme unity and the unity of divine operation, Thomas holds that all creaturely perfections exist in God eminently and without imperfection. Wisdom, goodness, and the rest are each the divine essence and really one, yet they differ in concept on account of the thing itself and not merely the reasoner. God is thus an analogical cause and exemplar through his attributes, and the view that the attributes differ only by their connoted effects is rejected. Conceptual plurality follows from real unity together with perfection, and the one divine operation is likewise conceptually manifold.
claims: Divine attributes are really one but conceptually distinct, grounded in God's perfection.
God causes analogically and is exemplar through his attributes.

ta-l1d2q1-Dd1e270.summary: Article 3, which Thomas treats as the key to Book I, asks whether the conceptual plurality of the attributes is in God or only in the intellect. Objections from Dionysius, Averroes, divine simplicity, and Damascene place it in the mind or in creatures. Sed contra arguments appeal to God's real perfection, creaturely imitation, analogy, and the parallel with paternity. Thomas defines a ratio and distinguishes three ways concepts are founded in things. He reconciles the negative and causal account of Avicenna and Maimonides with the eminence account of Dionysius and Anselm, and concludes that the attribute concepts are truly in God, with a proximate foundation in him. Their plurality arises because God's full perfection exceeds any single created concept; only the uncreated Word represents him perfectly. So the plurality is from our intellect as to its cause, and from God as to what corresponds to it. The replies distinguish knowing a cause through effects from its being true because of them, the subject of a concept from the foundation of its truth, and real from conceptual plurality.
claims: The rationes of the divine attributes are truly in God, founded proximately in his full perfection.
The plurality of these rationes arises because God's perfection exceeds every created concept.
The negative/causal and eminence accounts of divine names are reconcilable.

ta-l1d2q1-Dd1e397.summary: Article 4 asks whether the unity of the divine essence allows a plurality of persons. Objections argue from creatures, in which multiplying supposits multiplies the essence, from the identity of essence and supposit in God, and from the pointlessness of multiple supposits in a perfect nature. The sed contra arguments appeal to the self-diffusiveness of the good and to the perfection of beatitude and charity. Thomas grants the plurality of persons without hesitation, but on the basis of faith, judging the arguments not to be necessary demonstrations. The replies explain that the divine essence, being identical with its esse, can be communicated in its very being and so be numerically one in several supposits. Essence and supposit are conceptually distinct, so communicability belongs to one and not the other, and the persons' plurality is necessary of itself, not for an end.
claims: The plurality of persons in one essence is held on faith; the rational arguments are not demonstrative.
Because the divine essence is its esse, it can be numerically one in several supposits.

ta-l1d2q1-Dd1e437.summary: Article 5 asks whether the plurality of persons is real or only conceptual. Objections cite Damascene, Augustine's claim that the persons differ only in relatives, the conceptual status of personal properties, and the parity of relations with attributes. Thomas rejects a merely conceptual distinction as Sabellian. A divine relation is conceptually distinct from the essence but, as compared to its opposed correlative, really distinct from it. The persons are constituted and distinguished by that opposition, so their plurality is real. The replies reinterpret Damascene, note that 'res' is transcendental and covers both essential and relative realities, and explain why non-opposed attributes cannot distinguish supposits as opposed relations do.
claims: The plurality of persons is real, grounded in relative opposition.
A divine relation is really distinct from its correlative but only conceptually from the essence.
Non-opposed attributes cannot distinguish persons.

ta-l1d2q1-Dd1e506.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 2 glosses Lombard's text on the right way to investigate the Trinity and on its scriptural proofs. It covers the stages and purifications of faith and knowledge, Augustine's retractations, the plural predication of 'is' of the three persons, the significance of the names 'God' and 'Lord', Augustine's and Hilary's divergent readings of Genesis 1:26, and an allegorical reading of Proverbs 8 and other Old Testament texts as testimony to the Son and the two testaments.
claims: 'Is' is predicated plurally of the three persons.
'God' names the nature and 'Lord' names a relation founded on power.

ta-l1d2q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 2 lays the metaphysical foundations for the Trinitarian theology of Book I. The Prooemium sets the Sentences within an exitus–reditus scheme and places Book I as the study of the procession of persons in unity of essence. Article 1 proves God's unicity from the identity of essence and esse and the reduction of all multitude to one principle. Articles 2 and 3 develop Thomas's theory of the divine attributes: creaturely perfections pre-exist eminently in God, really one and conceptually many. The conceptual plurality is truly founded in God's full perfection, which exceeds every created concept, and on this basis Thomas reconciles Maimonides and Avicenna with Dionysius and Anselm. Article 4 holds on faith that the one essence, being its own esse, can exist numerically one in several supposits. Article 5 holds that the persons are really distinct through relative opposition, while each relation is only conceptually distinct from the essence. The Expositio glosses Lombard's text on investigating the Trinity and its scriptural proofs.
claims: God is one, since his essence is identical with his esse and cannot be multiplied.
The divine attributes are really one and conceptually distinct, with a proximate foundation in God's perfection.
The divine essence, being its esse, can be numerically one in several persons, as faith teaches.
The persons are really distinct through opposed relations, which are only conceptually distinct from the essence.
